extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism and creative writers interested in storytelling, myth, and moral/philosophical themes
extracted.subtask_description: A set of literary-critical and storytelling maxims drawn from Chesterton's essay on myth, paganism, Christianity, nationality, and the family, offering guidance on how stories resonate, how to portray character and culture, and what moral paradoxes make fiction effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotal vs Archetypal Myth distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two classes of popular tale: (1) anecdotal stories terminating in a repartee or singular incident (e.g., William Tell) that are plausible for a single person but not for many; and (2) archetypal incidents found in the stories of many heroes (e.g., Samson and Delilah) which are reasonable to imagine happening to many and are popular because they are not peculiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction when inventing or analysing tales: anecdotal tales gain popularity from peculiarity and uniqueness; archetypal myths gain popularity from universality and from expressing truths about people. When crafting legend-like material, decide whether you aim for a singular eccentricity or for a universal human pattern; the former persuades by specificity, the latter by telling a general truth about human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and multiplicity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a detail or mot appears in multiple sources or associated with many figures, it may be because it really happened to some unknown person or because it belongs to a kind of story that fits many lives; certain incidents are plausible for one hero but also plausible for several.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating believable anecdotes or attributing sayings, judge plausibility both for single occurrence (specificity) and for multiple occurrences (archetype). Recognize that repetition across contexts often signals an archetypal truth rather than fabrication—use repetition deliberately to suggest mythic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropomorphism as supernatural device
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive men pictured something semi-human at the back of all things, not to make phenomena more comprehensible but to make them more incomprehensible and mysterious; when nature looks like ourselves it becomes terrifying and uncanny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke the uncanny or the supernatural, give non-human things semi-human features. Anthropomorphism should increase mystery, not explain it away. Use human likeness to heighten fear or wonder: a tree that 'looks like a man' creates visceral reaction in the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity arises from truth about people
rubrics_metrics.description: Some stories (the archetypal kind) are popular because they 'tell the truth about people'—they are not peculiar but speak to common human experience (e.g., the ruin of great men by women across cultures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for thematic universality when seeking broad appeal: depict fundamental human patterns (love, weakness, betrayal) so stories resonate as 'true' across contexts. Use specific examples to illustrate universal truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid caricature when treating historical/cultural ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Paganism misrepresents ancient pagan civilizations as hedonistic and lawless, whereas historically they often upheld rigid dignity, responsibility, and civic obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fictionalizing or critiquing historical cultures or philosophies, avoid simplistic caricatures; research and portray the nuanced virtues and contradictions (e.g., pagans as reasonable and respectable). Misrepresentation reduces credibility and flattens moral complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-sequence caution (one came after the other)
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary fact about Christianity and Paganism is that one came after the other; treating them as parallel, interchangeable ideals ignores historical causality and the puzzle of why humanity adopted Christianity after paganism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical fiction or comparative cultural analysis, respect chronological development and causal relations rather than treating ideologies as timeless equals. Use sequence to explain shifts in sensibility or moral discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast of pagan 'rational' virtues and Christian 'mystical' virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Pagan (rational) virtues include justice and temperance; Christianity adopted these but also invented three mystical virtues—faith, hope, and charity—which are paradoxical, exuberant, and essentially unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building moral character or themes, differentiate between virtues grounded in measurable reason and virtues that are paradoxical and practical in extreme circumstances. Use faith/hope/charity to create moral tension and to reveal depths of character beyond rational calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox as a maker of moral truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Christian/mystical virtue is paradoxical: charity pardons the unpardonable, hope exists where things are hopeless, faith believes the incredible. These paradoxes are not mere rhetoric but practical necessities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In fiction, employ paradox to dramatize ethical and existential stakes. Characters who act against 'reason' in desperate circumstances—forgiveness, improbable hope, unprovable faith—signal profound moral truths and create memorable dramatic moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity (reverent agnosticism) as source of novel and fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity is described as a 'reverent agnosticism towards the complexity of the soul'; the novel and the art of fiction are creations of this mystical idea of charity, because fiction requires sympathy for complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create believable, rounded characters by granting them charity in narration—avoid reductive judgments; present inner conflicts sympathetically. Fiction that practices this kind of moral sympathy opens space for nuanced plots and psychological realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance defined by danger-enhanced delight
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance consists in thinking a thing more delightful because it is dangerous; it is linked to Christian ideas and is distinct from mere pleasantness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create romance in narrative, couple attraction with danger—make peril enhance desire or beauty. Use stakes and risk to intensify emotional responses rather than relying on idyllic safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility as imaginative and moral principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Humility—reducing the ego to zero—is the psychological discovery that renews wonder: it restores the freshness of perception so that ordinary things regain their marvel; humility is also practically necessary for learning and collective progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters' humility as a means of renewed perception and moral strength. Themes of humility can underpin transformations, growth, or sustained wonder in narrative. Avoid equating humility with mere asceticism; emphasize receptive, learning humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility enables progress and learning (avoid proud isolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest nations or people are those humble enough to learn from others (Prussia and Japan copied foreign excellence); pride and independent individualistic thinking hinder real progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In thematic design, show humility as productive—characters or societies that imitate and learn can triumph. Use contrast between arrogant isolation and humble imitation to dramatize success vs failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal capacity (original sin/equality) as characterization principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian realism holds that whatever moral dangers affect any man affect all men—each person can be criminal or heroic; there are no infallible 'wise few'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating immutable 'great men' archetypes; instead give ordinary characters both potential for heroism and foolishness. This egalitarian view supports more believable moral complexity and prevents hagiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationality as spiritual/psychological product, not racial fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Nationality is a spiritual product—a moment when many become a single will—independent of blood or race. National identity coheres by shared soul/volition rather than genetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting nations or national character, focus on shared beliefs, rituals, and collective will rather than essentializing race. Resist racialist or pseudo-scientific explanations; treat nationality as cultural and psychological cohesion useful for narrative conflict and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exoticizing folklore as uniquely ethnic
rubrics_metrics.description: Ireland's legends, songs, and visions are human rather than 'Celtic' in any exotic sense; calling a people 'Celtic' to mark them as strange or apart is a misreading—folk features are common human traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray folklore and mythic material as expressions of universal human traits. Avoid stereotyping or exoticizing a culture; present local color with respect and as part of broader human patterns to increase relatability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small community as richer source of human variety
rubrics_metrics.description: A person living in a small community knows more 'fierce varieties and uncompromising divergences of men' because companions are chosen for them; large societies enable cliques formed by sympathy and thus narrow the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small settings (villages, clans) to dramatize diverse interpersonal conflicts and compromises. To depict true sociability, show the frictions and renunciations that arise when people cannot self-select companions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic sociability requires discomfort and compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Sociability is full of discomforts, dangers, and renunciations; institutions (e.g., modern clubs) that prioritize comfort over argument make men unsociable rather than sociable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing social gatherings or institutions, foreground tensions, debates, and the costs of fellowship. Avoid portraying social spaces as only comfortable retreats; genuine relational drama emerges from imperfect, demanding interactions.
